{{Short description|Computational hardness assumption}}
The '''Decision Linear assumption''' ('''DLIN assumption''') is a [[computational hardness assumption]] used in [[elliptic curve cryptography]]. In particular, the DLIN assumption is useful in settings where the [[decisional Diffie&ndash;Hellman assumption]] does not hold (as is often the case in [[pairing-based cryptography]]). The Decision Linear assumption was introduced by [[Dan Boneh|Boneh]], Boyen, and Shacham.<ref name="BBS">[[Dan Boneh]], Xavier Boyen, Hovav Shacham: [https://crypto.stanford.edu/~dabo/papers/groupsigs.pdf Short Group Signatures]. CRYPTO 2004: 41&ndash;55</ref>

Informally the DLIN assumption states that given <math>(u, \, v, \, h, \, u^x, \, v^y)</math>, with <math>u, \, v, \, h</math> random group elements and <math>x, \, y</math> random exponents, it is hard to distinguish <math>h^{x+y}</math> from an independent random group element <math>\eta</math>.

==Motivation==
In symmetric [[pairing-based cryptography]] the group <math>G</math> is equipped with a pairing <math>e :G \times G \to T</math> which is [[Bilinear map|bilinear]]. This map gives an efficient algorithm to solve the [[Decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption|decisional Diffie-Hellman]] problem.<ref>John Bethencourt: [https://people.csail.mit.edu/alinush/6.857-spring-2015/papers/bilinear-maps.pdf Intro to Bilinear Maps]</ref> Given input <math>(g, \, g^a, \, g^b, \, h)</math>, it is easy to check if <math>h</math> is equal to <math>g^{ab}</math>. This follows by using the pairing: note that
:<math>e(g^a, g^b) = e(g,g)^{ab} = e(g,g^{ab}).</math>
Thus, if <math>h = g^{ab}</math>, then the values <math>e(g^a, g^b)</math> and <math>e(g,h)</math> will be equal.

Since this cryptographic assumption, essential to building [[ElGamal encryption]] and [[ElGamal signature scheme|signatures]], does not hold in this case, new assumptions are needed to build cryptography in symmetric bilinear groups. The DLIN assumption is a modification of Diffie-Hellman type assumptions to thwart the above attack.

==Formal definition==
Let <math>G</math> be a [[cyclic group]] of [[Prime number|prime]] [[Order (group theory)|order]] <math>p</math>. Let <math>u</math>, <math>v</math>, and <math>h</math> be uniformly random [[Generating set of a group|generators]] of <math>G</math>. Let <math>a,b</math> be uniformly random elements of <math>\{1, \, 2, \, \dots, \, p-1\}</math>. Define a distribution
:<math>D_1 = (u, \, v, \, h, \, u^a, \, v^b, \, h^{a+b}).</math>
Let <math>\eta</math> be another uniformly random element of <math>G</math>. Define another distribution
:<math>D_2 = (u, \, v, \, h, \, u^a, \, v^b, \, \eta).</math>
The Decision Linear assumption states that <math>D_1</math> and <math>D_2</math> are [[Computational indistinguishability|computationally indistinguishable]].

==Applications==
===Linear encryption===
Boneh, Boyen, and Shacham define a [[Public-key cryptography|public key encryption]] scheme by analogy to ElGamal encryption.<ref name="BBS"/> In this scheme, a public key is the generators <math>u,v,h</math>. The private key is two exponents such that <math>u^x = v^y = h</math>. Encryption combines a message <math>m \in G</math> with the public key to create a ciphertext
:<math>c := (c_1, \, c_2, \, c_3) = (u^a, \, v^b, \, m \cdot h^{a+b})</math>.
To decrypt the ciphertext, the private key can be used to compute
:<math>m' := c_3 \cdot (c_1^x \cdot c_2^y)^{-1}.</math>
To check that this encryption scheme is [[Correctness (computer science)|correct]], i.e. <math>m' = m</math> when both parties follow the protocol, note that
:<math>m' = c_3 \cdot (c_1^x \cdot c_2^y)^{-1} = m \cdot h^{a+b} \cdot ((u^a)^x \cdot (v^b)^y)^{-1} = m \cdot h^{a+b} \cdot ((u^x)^a \cdot (v^y)^b)^{-1}.</math>
Then using the fact that <math>u^x = v^y = h</math> yields
:<math>m' = m \cdot h^{a+b} \cdot (h^a \cdot h^b)^{-1} = m \cdot (h^{a+b} \cdot h^{-a-b}) = m.</math>
Further, this scheme is [[Ciphertext indistinguishability|IND-CPA]] [[Provable security|secure]] assuming that the DLIN assumption holds.

===Short group signatures===
Boneh, Boyen, and Shacham also use DLIN in a scheme for [[Group signature|group signatures]].<ref name="BBS"/> The signatures are called "short group signatures" because, with a standard [[security level]], they can be represented in only 250 [[Byte|bytes]].

Their protocol first uses linear encryption in order to define a special type of [[zero-knowledge proof]]. Then the [[Fiat–Shamir heuristic]] is applied to transform the proof system into a [[digital signature]]. They prove this signature fulfills the additional requirements of unforgeability, anonymity, and traceability required of a group signature.

Their proof relies on not only the DLIN assumption but also another assumption called the [[Strong Diffie–Hellman assumption|<math>q</math>-strong Diffie–Hellman assumption]]. It is proven in the [[Random oracle|random oracle model]].

===Other applications===
Since its definition in 2004, the Decision Linear assumption has seen a variety of other applications. These include the construction of a [[Pseudorandom function family|pseudorandom function]] that generalizes the [[Naor–Reingold pseudorandom function|Naor–Reingold construction]],<ref>Allison Bishop Lewko, [[Brent Waters]]: [https://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=1653662.1653677 Efficient pseudorandom functions from the decisional linear assumption and weaker variants]. CCS 2009: 112-120</ref> an [[attribute-based encryption]] scheme,<ref>Lucas Kowalczyk, Allison Bishop Lewko: [https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-662-48000-7_26 Bilinear Entropy Expansion from the Decisional Linear Assumption]. CRYPTO 2015: 524-541</ref> and a special class of [[Non-interactive zero-knowledge proof|non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs]].<ref>Benoît Libert, Thomas Peters, Marc Joye, [[Moti Yung]]: [https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-662-48797-6_28 Compactly Hiding Linear Spans]. ASIACRYPT 2015: 681-707</ref>
